chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Lawrence Brown's soft playing and Duke taking him for three trombones
summary: Brown strolled between tables playing quietly; McKinney would not hire him, so when Redman had three trombones Duke grabbed Brown.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Yeah. I never heard nothing that fast. I never heard a trombone player like that, not like Lawrence was playing in those days. Now, when I met him in Sebastian's Cotton Club, he was working with Les Hite. Now, in between dance sets of the show, there was a piano player named Harvey Brooks and Lawrence used to take his trombone and go around to the tables and play tunes. Whatever tune that the people wanted to hear Lawrence would play a tune for them. He could play that soft.

That's right, and could play that soft and had that much control. And Lawrence tried to get McKinney to get Lawrence then -- Excuse me -- but McKinney couldn't see three trombones and Don had the idea for it then. So when Don finally had three trombones in New York and Duke found out Don had three, Duke immediately when he went to California grabbed Lawrence Brown so he would have three.
So Duke is the one that got him, not McKinney.

And I have never worked beside a man that played as consistently and as beautiful as this man played. He had so much soul -- I have to say a soul. He could play blues, he could play melody, and he could almost cry on the trombone. He made such beautiful records.
